samples.summary: Comment/thread delete routes carry no author check — any workspace member (or any write-scoped API key) can delete another user's comments
samples.evidence: `@Delete(':threadId')` (deleteThread) and `@Delete(':threadId/comments/:commentId')` (deleteComment) are the only two handlers in the new controller that do not take `@Req()` at all: they resolve nothing about the caller and hand the thread id straight to `applyDeleteThread` / `applyDeleteComment` (packages/backend/src/yorkie/comment-ops.ts), which delete unconditionally. The product's stated rule is author-only: the editor gates edit and delete on `c.author.userId === currentUserId` (packages/frontend/src/components/comments/components/CommentThreadCard.tsx:92). Attack: any member of the workspace, or an agent holding a `write`-scoped API key minted by any member, issues `DELETE /api/v1/workspaces/{ws}/documents/{doc}/comments/{threadId}` and silently destroys an entire review conversation authored by someone else — including deleting the opening comment of a thread, which `applyDeleteComment` escalates into deleting the whole thread. Nothing in the request or the CRDT records who did it. Mitigating context I confirmed and am reporting honestly: the Yorkie auth webhook grants workspace members `rw` on every document in the workspace (packages/backend/src/document/yorkie-auth.controller.ts:196-206), so a hostile editor client could already write the same CRDT deletion directly; the author rule has never had server-side enforcement. This new path is nevertheless the first server-side writer, i.e. the first place the rule *could* be enforced, and it ships without it while reading as a governed API surface.

read comment-ops.ts applyDeleteThread/applyDeleteComment for any author comparison

samples.summary: `parseImages` stores `src` verbatim with no scheme/origin validation, letting an API caller plant arbitrary third-party URLs that every viewer's browser then fetches
samples.evidence: `src: requireString(i.src, 'src')` accepts any non-empty string — no `http(s)`-only check, no same-origin check, no length cap. The controller writes it straight into the CRDT (`ws.images[image.id] = image`, worksheet-images.controller.ts:112). Every other writer of this field holds the URL to first-party workspace image URLs: the editor only ever stores `result.url` from `uploadImageFile` (packages/frontend/src/app/spreadsheet/sheet-view.tsx:551), and the codebase treats first-party-ness as an explicit security boundary elsewhere — `isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` (packages/frontend/src/api/share-image-url.ts:40) and `parseImageRef` (packages/backend/src/document/document-image-refs.ts:66-95) both refuse foreign origins by design. Attack: a member with a write-scoped API key PUTs `{"images":[{"id":"x","src":"https://attacker.example/px.gif",...}]}`; thereafter every workspace member who opens the sheet, and every anonymous share-link viewer, issues a request to the attacker's host from `` (packages/frontend/src/app/spreadsheet/image-object-layer.tsx:216), leaking viewer IP/User-Agent/Referer and giving a read receipt per viewer. `data:` and `javascript:` URLs are equally accepted; they do not execute in an `` today, but nothing constrains the value if this field ever reaches an HTML/SVG or export context. Secondary: no cap on `src`/`alt` length or on the number of images, so one 25MB request (the configured body limit) can be dumped into the CRDT. Noted for the verifier: the slides/board content PUT already stores element `data.src` unvalidated, so this is a widening of an existing gap rather than a wholly new one.

samples.summary: `worksheetOrThrow` accepts inherited object keys as a worksheet, so `tabId=__proto__` reaches a write of `ws.images = {}` onto the prototype
samples.evidence: `const worksheet = root.sheets?.[tabId]; if (!worksheet) throw new NotFoundException(...)` treats any truthy lookup as a worksheet, including inherited members. With `tabId` = `__proto__` a plain-object root yields `Object.prototype`; with `constructor` it yields the `Object` function. `setImages` then executes `ws.images = {}` inside `doc.update` (line 110-112) against that value — i.e. `Object.prototype.images = {}` — and returns 200 with the echoed payload for a write that never touched the document. Reachability in production depends on how the Yorkie object proxy's `get` trap answers `__proto__` (likely `undefined`, which would make this unreachable), which I could not verify — the SDK is not vendored in this tree — hence the low confidence. Note the same shape guards itself in comments.controller.ts:230-236 only by accident: `sheetCellAnchor` reads `worksheet.rowOrder`, which is absent on `Object.prototype`, so it 400s first. The pattern is copied verbatim from the pre-existing `ApiV1WorksheetChartsController.worksheetOrThrow` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/worksheet-charts.controller.ts:49-56), so it is not introduced here, only duplicated. A `tabId` allowlist check against `root.tabOrder`/`Object.hasOwn` would close both.
searchedFor: read worksheet-images.controller.ts worksheetOrThrow and setImages
compared with worksheet-charts.controller.ts:49 for precedent
traced comments.controller.ts createThread sheet branch for the same lookup
glob for a vendored @yorkie-js/sdk to inspect the proxy get trap (not present)

samples.summary: Server-side comment notifications bypass `UserThrottlerGuard`; only the shared 120/min IP bucket bounds mention fan-out from a write-scoped API key
samples.evidence: `this.notificationService.createFromComment(actorId, plan)` is called directly, so the per-user limiter that guards the browser's report endpoint (`UserThrottlerGuard` on `POST /notifications/comment`, packages/backend/src/notification/notification.controller.ts:34) never runs — the change's own docs state this as accepted (docs/design/notifications.md, "What it is *not* subject to is `UserThrottlerGuard`"). What remains is the global IP-keyed `ThrottlerGuard` at 120 req/min (packages/backend/src/app.module.ts:97-102). Each accepted request can carry up to `MAX_RECIPIENTS` (20) recipients via `@[x](id)` mentions with an attacker-chosen `preview`, and `dedupeKey` is the freshly minted `commentId`, so nothing collapses the repeats: ~2400 inbox rows/min per source address from one write-scoped key, each pushing an SSE summary. Bounded but not user-bounded, and the bound is per-IP rather than per-key, which the guard it replaced exists precisely to avoid.
searchedFor: read notification.service.createFromComment for caps (MAX_RECIPIENTS=20, sanitizePreview)
grep SkipThrottle|@Throttle across packages/backend/src/api/v1 (no override on the comments controller)
read app.module.ts ThrottlerModule.forRoot default bucket
read user-throttler.guard.ts and notification.controller.ts to confirm which routes it guards

samples.summary: Notification preview carries the raw mention markup, unlike the frontend which flattens it — lets a comment author choose the display name shown in someone else's inbox
samples.evidence: The backend plan sets `preview: comment.body` (and `thread.comments[0]?.body` for a resolve), whereas the frontend's equivalent runs `mentionBodyToPlainText(body)` first (packages/frontend/src/components/comments/notify.ts:36). A mention is stored as `@[display](userId)` and the display half is entirely attacker-chosen, so an API-authored comment such as `@[Security Team](9) approve this` renders in the recipient's dropdown with the raw markup and an arbitrary name the attacker picked, next to their own (correct) actor name. `sanitizePreview` strips bidi/zero-width and control characters but does nothing about the markup itself. Low impact — social engineering inside the notification line only — but it is a divergence from the sanitisation the other writer applies.
searchedFor: read planCommentNotifications in comments.controller.ts
read packages/frontend/src/components/comments/notify.ts preview()
read sanitizePreview in notification.service.ts

samples.summary: `unwrapJson` now runs a repairing JSON parser over attacker-influenceable document content and silently falls back on any failure
samples.evidence: The bare `JSON.parse(str)` was replaced by `parseJsonSnapshot(str)` inside `try/catch`, which on a "control character" SyntaxError re-parses the string after rewriting it with `escapeControlCharsInJson` (line 43) — a hand-rolled quote/backslash scanner over content that includes user-written cell values and image metadata, and whose output is then trusted as the document (`tabs.controller.ts` duplicate writes the unwrapped worksheet back into a new tab). Any desynchronisation of the scanner's `inString` state between the real serializer's escaping and this repair is a parser differential: the repaired document is not the stored one. I could not construct a concrete payload — Yorkie appears to escape `"` correctly and only leaks raw control characters — so this is a suspicion about the shape of the change, not a demonstrated forgery. The `catch { return detachYorkieValue(value) }` fallback also converts any other parse failure into a silently different value rather than an error.
searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-json.ts in full
traced unwrapJson callers: tabs.controller.ts duplicate, worksheet-images.controller.ts getImages, board-tree.ts, worksheet-charts.controller.ts

samples.summary: `normalizeBody` imposes no maximum comment length, so one authenticated request can push a 25MB body into the CRDT
samples.evidence: `normalizeBody` only type-checks and rejects whitespace-only input; there is no upper bound. The configured body limit is `JSON_BODY_LIMIT` (25MB, packages/backend/src/main.ts:49), and the comment routes sit on the default 120 req/min bucket, so a write-scoped API key can grow a document's CRDT without limit. Storage/availability cost only — `sanitizePreview` caps what reaches the notification row at 200 chars — but no other validation on this surface (`parseImages`, `parsePdfAnchor`) caps a string either.
searchedFor: read normalizeBody and buildThread/buildReply in comment-ops.ts
read requireString/parsePdfAnchor in comments.controller.ts for length caps
read main.ts bodyParser limits

verdict.reason: The factual absence is real — deleteThread (comments.controller.ts:388-401) and deleteComment (:403-431) take no @Req() and call applyDeleteThread/applyDeleteComment (comment-ops.ts:238-263) unconditionally, and neither WorkspaceScopeGuard (workspace-scope.guard.ts:32-46) nor ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard (api-key-write-scope.guard.ts:38-49) performs any per-comment author check. However it is not a blocking authorization defect under the security rubric, because no principal gains authority it does not already hold: (a) any authenticated user can mint a Yorkie token (auth.controller.ts:68-73) and the auth webhook grants rw on EVERY document in a workspace they are a member of, with the code explicitly noting there is no per-member viewer role (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:188-207), so a member can already delete any thread by writing the CRDT directly; (b) API keys can only be minted by a workspace owner (api-key.controller.ts:33 assertOwner), and such a credential already passes isDocumentManager and can delete the entire document with all its comments (documents.controller.ts:169-198); (c) cross-tenant IDOR is closed since loadCommentableType scopes the lookup by workspaceId (comments.controller.ts:110-113) behind the membership guard. The author-only rule exists solely as a client UI affordance (CommentThreadCard.tsx:92) and has never been a server-enforced boundary, so adding it here would be defense-in-depth hardening (minor), not the closing of a privilege escalation or IDOR. No new bypass, no boundary crossed.

verdict.reason: The absence claim is factually accurate: worksheet-images.ts:40-105 stores `src` via requireString only (no scheme/origin check, no length or count cap), the controller writes it straight into the CRDT (worksheet-images.controller.ts:99-113), the render path fetches it unfiltered (image-object-layer.tsx:195-216, image-cache.ts:46-93), and there is no app-wide img-src CSP (only frame-ancestors on cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:166). I found no counterexample validation anywhere in the chain. It is nevertheless not blocking under this lens's rubric: (1) it opens no trust boundary that is not already open - the editor writes the identical field directly into the Yorkie CRDT client-side (sheet-view.tsx:549) and the server's realtime gate inspects only document id + verb, never content (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:170-221), so any write-scoped API-key member, and even an anonymous share-link *editor* (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:217), can already push an arbitrary `src` via pushpull; a check in parseImages closes none of that. (2) The security-relevant consequence - share-token exfiltration to a foreign origin - is deliberately guarded at consumption (share-image-url.ts:18-57, image-cache.ts:29-48) and at copy time (document-image-refs.ts:51-90), and image-cache.ts:86-91 explicitly anticipates third-party hosts as benign. (3) Residual harm is a tracking pixel / read receipt planted by an already-authorized writer, with no HTML/SVG injection sink (img src only; data:/javascript: do not execute there) and no server-side fetch of `src` (no SSRF) - i.e. hardening (minor), not auth bypass, secret exposure, injection, or a broken crypto check. The missing alt/src/count caps are availability and are equally unbounded on the realtime path.
